title: How it is spoken
description: Ide is one dialect with a defined sound: read town by town out of the Igbo varieties, then written by its own rules. This page is how it sounds and how it is said.
html:
The sound rules

A form containing <code>gh</code> is never an Ide word.

RuleWhat it saysExample
(N)(C)Vevery syllableAn optional nasal, an optional consonant, a vowel. No closed syllable, ever — a source word ending in a consonant takes a vowel.
gh → ya source gh is written yagha → aya war; Mkpọọ jàghe → jaye open.
r → la source r is written lwere → weli; dùùrù → dulu adult; afere → afele plate.
h → f / va source h is written f, and Northern Anambra writes it vhụ → fụ; ahịa market → Ogbunike afịa, Aguleri and Anam avịa; aha → Ogbunike afà, Aguleri avà. The shift runs /ɦ/ → /f/ → /v/: that is the Anambra North and Central fusion — the f of the Central belt and the v of the North are one sound at two stages. There is no bare h and no bare r in the dialect.
chi / sichi is the word; si is how it is widely saidThe personal force. Both are Ide: chi is the form, si the common pronunciation.
nyny, never ñnyo, nye, anya.
dotted vowelsthe dot is a letter, not an accentụkwụ foot is not ukwu; ọnụ mouth is not onu neck.

The voice

311 words carry their own recording, and the player shows the shape of the sound. The rule here is that the recording must say the word shown. It costs most of the audio, and it is the honest position: every one of the 46,419 recordings in the source is an izugbe headword from the nkowaokwu/ibo-dict corpus, and not one is attached to a dialect spelling. So a dialect form paired with its “own” recording was in fact playing the central Igbo word — which is exactly what it sounded like. 6,273 pairs showed one word and played another. Only words where the sound, the spelling and the Ide lexicon all agree are carried here with audio; the rest are on the site without it rather than mislabelled.

311 words carry a recording.
